original_comment:
June 15, 2026 
 
The Honorable Mehmet Oz, MD, MBA 
Administrator 
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services 
U.S. Department of Health and Human Services  
7500 Security Boulevard 
Baltimore, MD 21244 
 
The Honorable Thomas Keane, MD, MBA 
National Coordinator for Health Information Technology 
Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology 
330 C Street SW 
Washington, DC 20201 
 
RE: Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Patient Protection and 
Affordable Care Act; Interoperability Standards and Prior 
Authorization for Drugs for Medicare Advantage Organizations, 
Medicaid Managed Care Plans, State Medicaid Agencies, 
Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) Agencies and CHIP 
Managed Care Entities, and Issuers of Qualified Health Plans on 
the Federally-Facilitated Exchanges [CMS-0062-P] 
 
Dear Administrator Oz and National Coordinator Keane: 
 
On behalf of the more than 5,000 members of the American Academy of 
Hospice and Palliative Medicine (AAHPM), thank you for the opportunity 
to comment in response to the Interoperability Standards and Prior 
Authorization for Drugs proposed rule referenced above. AAHPM is the 
professional organization for physicians specializing in Hospice and 
Palliative Medicine (HPM). Our membership also includes nurses, social 
workers, spiritual care providers, pharmacists, and other health 
professionals deeply committed to improving quality of life for the 
expanding population of patients facing serious illness as well as their 
families and caregivers. Together, we strive to advance the field and 
ensure that patients across all communities and geographies have access 
to high-quality palliative and hospice care.  
 
 
Overall, AAHPM appreciates CMS’s proposals that extend prior authorization standards and electronic 
prior authorization processing requirements to drugs covered by impacted payers.  Prior authorization 
requirements for drugs contribute to significant burden for our members – and potential harm to their 
patients – particularly as they apply to medications needed to alleviate pain and other distressing 
symptoms associated with serious illness.  A single prior authorization request can take an hour or more 
of physician or clinical staff time to process, diverting attention and resources away from patient care. 
Furthermore, prior authorization requirements delay patient access to medically necessary and 
appropriate care in the best-case scenarios, while denying access altogether in the worst. Either outcome 
can lead to significant patient harm, particularly for patients with serious illness who are often contending 
with medical complexity, pain, and restricted function that could be ameliorated with additional 
treatments. Imposing new requirements on plans will therefore help to reduce burden, facilitate 
transparency, and increase patient access to medically necessary medications.  At the same time, we also 
call on CMS to establish and articulate strong enforcement mechanisms that ensure payers adhere to the 
new requirements to improve prior authorization processes for prescription drugs.  
Summary of Key Messages and Recommendations 
AAHPM offers the following key messages and recommendations, which are further detailed in our 
comments below.  
• 
Interoperability Standards. CMS should finalize its proposal to require impacted payers to 
implement the Prior Authorization application program interface (API) or the National Council for 
Prescription Drug Programs (NCPDP) SCRIPT standard to enable processing of electronic prior 
authorization requests for drugs covered under a medical or pharmacy benefit, respectively.  
• 
Denial Reasons. CMS should finalize its proposal for impacted payers to provide a specific reason 
to providers when denying a prior authorization request for drugs, regardless of the method used 
to send the prior authorization request or decision. 
• 
Prior Authorization Decision Timeframes. CMS should finalize prior authorization decision 
timeframes of 48 hours for standard non-drug requests and 24 hours for expedited requests for 
all impacted payers. CMS should finalize consistent prior authorization decision timeframes of 24 
hours for both standard and expedited drug-related prior authorization requests and 
expeditiously undertake future rulemaking to require the same decision timeframe for Medicare 
Advantage (MA) plans. 
• 
Prior Authorization Metrics. CMS should finalize its proposals for updating public reporting of 
prior authorization metrics for non-drug items and services, including to incorporate drugs into 
the existing prior authorization metrics. CMS should expand public reporting requirements to 
include prior authorization data on specific categories of items and services for non-drug items 
and services and require public reporting of drug-related prior authorization requests at the 
category and class level. 
• 
Updates to APIs.  
o CMS should finalize its proposals to add prior authorization information for drugs to the 
Patient Access, Provider Access, and Payer-to-Payer APIs. CMS should also monitor the 
impacts of the implementation of the APIs (including with new drug prior authorization 
data if finalized) and update its policies, including physician payment policies, to account 
for potential increased burden and costs borne by physician practices. 
o CMS should not finalize its proposal to remove drug formulary information as data 
required to make available via the Provider Access and Payer-to-Payer APIs for MA 
organizations, state Medicaid and CHIP FFS programs, Medicaid managed care plans, and 
CHIP managed care entities. 
• 
Electronic Event Notification.  
o CMS should clarify that hospices are included among the post-acute care providers to 
which hospitals must attempt to send electronic event notifications.  
o CMS should ensure that hospitals are aware of the need to send electronic event 
notifications to patients’ palliative care teams, when such teams are actively managing 
patients’ care.  
o CMS should work with Congress to secure resources for hospices to make the necessary 
information technology investments to accommodate electronic event notifications 
adopt certified electronic health record technology.  
• 
Step Therapy. AAHPM supports the idea of plans obtaining access to patient medication history 
to automate utilization management processes and bypass repeated step therapy requirements 
when patients move from one plan to another. 
• 
Prior Authorization for Durable Medical Equipment. AAHPM supports the use of technology to 
reduce burden associated with the prior authorization process for DMEPOS items and encourages 
CMS to pursue additional avenues to leverage technology in such a manner.  
Interoperability Standards and Electronic Prior 
Authorization for Drugs  
CMS proposes to require impacted payers to use either the Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources 
(FHIR®) standards and Implementation Guides (IGs) required for the Prior Authorization API or the NCPDP 
SCRIPT standard depending on whether the drugs are covered under a medical benefit or a pharmacy 
benefit, as well as the NCPDP Formulary and Benefit standard and the NCPDP Real-Time Prescription 
Benefit standard.  AAHPM supports these proposals, which we believe would reduce prior authorization 
burden by increasing transparency and streamlining prior authorization processes, as well as promote 
electronic exchange of formulary and utilization management information, and we recommend that CMS 
finalize these policies as proposed.   
 
Improving Communications and Decision Timeframes for 
Prior Authorizations  
Specific Denial Reasons 
AAHPM supports CMS’s proposal that, beginning October 1, 2027, state Medicaid and CHIP FFS programs, 
Medicaid managed care plans, CHIP managed care entities, and Qualified Health Plan (QHP) issues on the 
federally-facilitated exchanges (FFEs) be required to provide a specific reason to providers when denying a 
prior authorization request for drugs, regardless of the method used to send the prior authorization 
request or decision.  Finalizing this proposal would give providers clearer information when assessing 
whether to seek a reconsideration. Additionally, this proposal is important for practices that may not 
have the technological capacity to submit prior authorization requests electronically. For example, many 
palliative care practices may not have access to certified electronic health record technology (CEHRT) 
needed to support the Prior Authorization API or the NCPDP SCRIPT standard given that few electronic 
health record (EHR) vendors have developed CEHRT tailored for use in hospice and palliative care.   
 
Prior Authorization Decision Timeframes 
AAHPM also appreciates CMS’s efforts to formalize prior authorization decision timeframes, including for 
non-drug items and services reviewed by several payer types (Medicaid and CHIP fee-for-service; QHPs 
on FFEs), as well as for drug-related prior authorizations across plan types.  However, as we previously 
indicated, we are concerned that the timelines proposed for non-drug items and services are not 
sufficiently responsive to patients’ needs to access treatment, and that the proposed timelines that vary 
across payer type are too complicated and could lead to confusion and delayed access.  We note that 
timely access is particularly important for seriously ill patients who face severe, painful, and/or 
debilitating conditions, for whom each day of treatment delay can result in increased harm.  We therefore 
reiterate our previously-submitted recommendation that – for medical services across all payer types – 
CMS finalize prior authorization decision timeframes of 48 hours for standard requests and 24 hours for 
expedited requests. And for drug-related prior authorization requests, we recommend that CMS finalize a 
uniform prior authorization decision timeframe across all impacted payer types of 24 hours for both 
standard and expedited decisions, which would be consistent with statutory requirements for covered 
outpatient drugs in the Medicaid program and CMS’s proposal for State CHIP fee-for-service programs. 
We note that the disparate timelines that CMS proposes for making decisions on drug-related prior 
authorization requests across different payer types is likely to result in confusion and differential access 
to medically necessary medications. Finally, in response to CMS’s comment solicitation on prior 
authorization decision timeframes for Medicare Advantage plans, we also recommend that CMS 
implement in future rulemaking final policies that require responses to all prior authorization requests for 
drugs no later than 24 hours, in order to maintain consistency across regulated programs and maximize 
access for Medicare patients requiring access to prescription medications; such regulations should be 
finalized as expeditiously as possible.  
 
Prior Authorization Metrics  
CMS proposes to amend prior authorization metrics related to non-drug items and services that impacted 
payers are currently required to report, to add four new metrics and to require impacted payers to report 
a numeric count of prior authorization requests in addition to percentages.  CMS also proposes to 
incorporate drugs into the existing prior authorization metrics and to require impacted payers to begin 
public reporting of these prior authorization metrics for all drugs beginning in 2028. CMS notes that 
Covered Part D drugs are not included in its proposal because they are covered in other reporting 
regulations, but CMS does propose that MA organizations would include any drugs payable under Part B 
that require prior authorization.  
 
AAHPM supports CMS’s proposals for public reporting of additional prior authorization metrics for non-
drugs items and services, as well as CMS’s proposals to incorporate drugs into the existing prior 
authorization metrics.  However, we continue to recommend that CMS further refine its proposal to 
require public reporting of specific categories of non-drug items and services, rather than just aggregate 
data, as well as public reporting of drug-related prior authorization requests at the category and class 
level.  Such information would help stakeholders better understand plans’ prior authorization practices 
and increase efficiency around the submission of prior authorization requests. Standardization of 
reporting across plans would also facilitate stakeholders’ ability to compare and contrast plans on their 
prior authorization metrics and identify trends in the use of prior authorization across plans and regions.  
 
Updates to Patient Access, Provider Directory, Provider 
Access, and Payer-to-Payer APIs; API Usage Metrics 
CMS proposes to require impacted payers to add information about prior authorization requests and 
decisions for all drugs available to patients via the Patient Access, Provider Access, and Payer-to-Payer 
APIs.  AAHPM supports the addition of prior authorization information for drugs to the Patient Access, 
Provider Access, and Payer-to-Payer APIs. However, AAHPM continues to be concerned about potential 
burdens and costs that may be associated with the addition of this information – for example related to 
higher frequency of patient inquiries, increased time spent reviewing patient data, and costs associated 
with technology upgrades. We therefore again recommend that CMS monitor the impacts of 
implementing the APIs, including with the proposed new drug prior authorization data, and update its 
policies, including physician payment policies, as needed to account for such increased demand.  
 
CMS also proposes to remove drug formulary information in the Provider Access API and Payer-to-Payer 
APIs for MA organizations, state Medicaid and CHIP FFS programs, Medicaid managed care plans, and 
CHIP managed care entities.  AAHPM opposes this proposal and urges CMS not to finalize it. While CMS 
claims that providers can access formulary information through other routes, e.g., payer websites and 
standard payer communications materials, our members report that such formulary information is not 
easy to access or understand for practicing physicians, particularly when considering plans may have 
multiple formularies with different cost-sharing amounts depending on which specific benefit package 
applies to a beneficiary.  Instead, providers are routinely checking with pharmacies to ensure they have 
accurate coverage and cost-sharing information based on the beneficiary, prescription, and plan.  Having 
data on covered drugs and cost-sharing specific to each beneficiary through a Payer Access API would 
facilitate physicians’ ability to assist their patients in obtaining effective, affordable prescription drug 
options.  
 
Request for Information: Electronic Event Notifications for 
Value-Based Care and Care Coordination 
CMS seeks comment on many aspects of its current requirements for hospitals to make a reasonable 
effort to send electronic event notifications to all applicable post-acute care providers, as well as to PCPs 
or other practitioners/groups identified by the patient as primarily responsible for their care.   
 
AAHPM encourages CMS to clarify that hospices are included among the post-acute care providers to 
which hospitals must attempt to send electronic event notifications.  When reviewing the regulation text, 
there was no clear reference to hospice providers or definition of post-acute care provider that we could 
readily identify.  We believe it is important for hospices to receive such information to ensure they have a 
fulsome picture of the care their patients are seeking, including if such care results in disenrollment from 
the hospice benefit.  We also recommend that CMS ensure that hospitals check to determine if a patient 
is enrolled in hospice and, if so, have a way to determine which hospice is responsible for the patient’s 
care. Our members have reported that while hospitals may sometimes send electronic notifications to 
hospices, there can be a breakdown if hospitals cannot accurately attribute the patient to a particular 
hospice.   
 
We also highlight the role that community-based palliative care teams in managing the care of patients 
with serious illness, including to engage in detailed and skilled communication with patients and families 
to elicit goals and preferences; conduct expert assessment and management of physical, psychological, 
and other sources of suffering; and coordinate care with the patient’s primary care and specialty care 
providers across the multiple settings (e.g., hospital, post-acute care, ambulatory clinics, home) that 
patients traverse throughout the course of a serious illness.  We therefore encourage CMS to ensure that 
hospitals are aware of the need to send notifications to patients’ palliative care teams, when such teams 
are actively managing patients’ care. 
 
And while we underscore the need to share communications with hospices and palliative care teams, 
when applicable, we also note that these providers and practitioners may have challenges receiving 
electronic event notifications to the extent they rely on certified electronic heath record technology 
(CEHRT). This is because CEHRT remains largely unsuitable for hospices due to their historic exclusion 
from the Medicare and Medicaid Electronic Health Record Incentive Program. As a result, EHR vendors 
have not developed CEHRT that is applicable to hospice settings, and hospices and their affiliated 
palliative care practices have not been able to make the investments in core health information 
technology necessary to accommodate electronic event notifications.  In lieu of having access to their 
own CEHRT, we have also heard that hospices may gain access to electronic event notifications by 
participating in hospitals’ electronic communications platforms, which can be expensive for hospices. 
While we agree that access to such information is valuable for hospices, we are concerned about the 
costs that hospices must bear.  We therefore recommend that CMS work with Congress to secure 
resources and incentives for hospices to make the necessary information technology investments (IT) to 
accommodate electronic event notifications and adopt CEHRT that is relevant to their practice, similar to 
investments made under the EHR Incentive Program. Without such investments, we urge against any 
policy changes that would require hospices to bear new costs related to participation in additional 
electronic platforms.  
Request for Information: Step Therapy  
CMS solicits comment on whether increased interoperability of IT systems across payers could be used to 
make utilization management policies, such as step therapy, more transparent.  AAHPM has deep 
concerns with the use of step therapy to restrict patients’ access to medically necessary medications, 
particularly for patients with serious illness who may struggle to find the right array of medications to 
manage the complex and manifold symptoms. In serious illness care, we typically see step therapy 
requirements associated with long-acting opioids, anti-emetics, and bowel medications. However, to the 
extent that step therapy requirements are in place, AAHPM agrees that increased transparency through 
the use of IT systems could facilitate patient access.  We particularly support the idea of plans obtaining 
access to patient medication history to automate the utilization management process and bypass 
repeated step therapy requirements when patients move from one plan to another. We note that 
technology solutions should be able to easily mine data for information on prior prescriptions, such that 
additional documentation would not be required from health care teams. We also encourage CMS to 
consider solutions for originating plans to digitize and transmit data related to tried-and-failed over-the-
counter medications, which also often factor into step therapy regimens, in order to ensure that receiving 
plans have a full picture of patients’ medication histories and that step therapy burden is minimized to 
the full extent possible.  
 
We also take this opportunity to highlight how availability of formulary data via the Provider Access API 
and the Payer-to-Payer API would help to facilitate exchange and management of data to support 
automated step therapy determinations, particularly in situations where patients are moving from payer 
to payer. Although formulary information might already be available through other means, such as payer 
websites and standard communication materials, ensuring that it is easily accessible and transmissible 
through EHRs, alongside other related patient and drug information required through these APIs, is 
critical to ensuring a more seamless process going forward.  We therefore reiterate our concern with 
CMS’s proposal to remove formular information from these APIs.  
Request for Information: Laboratory Tests and DMEPOS 
Items 
CMS solicits information on how prior authorization for durable medical equipment, prosthetics, 
orthotics, and supplies (DMEPOS) impacts patient care and health care provider burden, and if there are 
opportunities to mitigate burden.   
 
As with general prior authorization requirements, prior authorization requirements for DMEPOS items in 
particular present significant challenges for palliative care teams.  Walkers, wheelchairs, and hospital 
beds are commonly needed for palliative care patients, but some palliative care programs simply lack the 
staffing to process prior authorization requests. As a result, many are unable to connect their patients to 
these necessary supplies and equipment.  
 
AAHPM believes that technology could be used to reduce burden associated with the prior authorization 
process for DMEPOS items, and we encourage CMS to pursue additional avenues to leverage technology 
to reduce burden. For example, algorithms could be used to proactively identify patients who are likely to 
benefit from DMEPOS items and supplies and authorize their use in advance; for example, a patient who 
is hospitalized for two weeks, requires physical therapy, and is documented as being non-ambulatory 
could be proactively offered an authorization for a wheelchair. At a minimum, using technology to offer 
real-time prior authorization in such scenarios would help to mitigate burden.  
 
CMS also asks how issues associated with prior authorization impact the healthcare workforce and 
retention of skilled health care professionals.  Prior authorization processes contribute to frustration and 
dissatisfaction for health care professionals at all levels, whether associated with DMEPOS items or 
otherwise.  To illustrate: 
• 
Physicians’ time is disrespected when they must take time away from patients to wait on hold for 
a phone call with some who has less specialty expertise on a prior authorization determination.  
• 
Nurses who are capable of higher levels of care spend time filling out paperwork, regurgitating 
provider documentation in the format that is required for each payer.  
• 
Even front desk staff face backlash from patients who feel that prior authorization processes 
should happen faster.   
 
No one enters a profession in health care aiming to devote their time to duplicative paperwork that 
justifies their patients’ needs. As a result, prior authorization demands are frequently cited as a major 
reason physicians and clinical staff leave the medical workforce.   
 
For these reasons, AAHPM appreciates CMS’s continued focus on streamlining prior authorization 
processes and reducing prior authorization burden, including for DMEPOS items. AAHPM stands ready to 
serve as a resource as CMS continues this important work. 
 
* * * * * 
 
Thank you, again, for the opportunity to provide feedback on this proposed rule. If you have any 
questions, please feel free to reach out to Wendy Chill, Senior Director, Health Policy and Government 
Relations, with any questions at wchill@aahpm.org or (847) 375-6733.  
 
Sincerely, 
 
Kimberly Curseen, MD, FAAHPM 
President, American Academy of Hospice and Palliative Medicine
analysis:
# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** American Academy of Hospice and Palliative Medicine (AAHPM), signed by Kimberly Curseen, MD, FAAHPM, President.
- **Stakeholder type:** Professional Association; Healthcare Provider.
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** Represents more than 5,000 hospice and palliative medicine physicians and interdisciplinary serious-illness care professionals, including nurses, social workers, spiritual care providers, pharmacists, and other clinicians.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

AAHPM supports CMS proposals to extend electronic prior authorization standards to drugs and to require specific denial reasons, but asks CMS to strengthen timelines, transparency, enforcement, and API policy. The commenter emphasizes the serious harm that PA delays can cause for patients with serious illness, particularly for medications used to alleviate pain and distressing symptoms.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; API-USAGE-METRICS; PATIENT/PROVIDER/PAYER-TO-PAYER API drug PA data as related to FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; GENERAL RFIs on electronic event notifications, step therapy, and DMEPOS.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** No CFR citations emphasized in the commenter text; references proposed October 1, 2027 implementation date and CMS-0062-P.
- **Standards referenced:** FHIR; Da Vinci Prior Authorization API framework; NCPDP SCRIPT; NCPDP Formulary and Benefit; NCPDP Real-Time Prescription Benefit; CEHRT; APIs for Patient Access, Provider Access, and Payer-to-Payer exchange.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Electronic Prior Authorization for Drugs**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** Drug PA requirements impose clinical burden and delay medications needed for pain and symptom relief in serious illness care.
- **Specific request:** Finalize requirements for impacted payers to implement the Prior Authorization API for medical benefit drugs and NCPDP SCRIPT for pharmacy benefit drugs.

**Topic 2: Specific Denial Reasons**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DENIAL-REASONS
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** Specific denial reasons help clinicians decide whether to seek reconsideration and are particularly important for practices lacking electronic PA capability.
- **Specific request:** Finalize the requirement that payers provide specific reasons for drug PA denials regardless of submission method.

**Topic 3: Shorter and More Uniform Decision Timeframes**
- **Provision ID:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Seriously ill patients face harm when access is delayed; varying timelines by payer type are confusing and may create unequal access.
- **Specific request:** Require 48 hours for standard non-drug requests and 24 hours for expedited non-drug requests; require 24 hours for both standard and expedited drug PA requests across impacted payers, and pursue future MA rulemaking for the same standard.

**Topic 4: Prior Authorization Metrics and Granularity**
- **Provision ID:** API-USAGE-METRICS; TRANSPARENCY
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Aggregate reporting obscures meaningful patterns in PA burden and patient access barriers.
- **Specific request:** Finalize new metrics, incorporate drugs into PA reporting, report non-drug categories, and report drug PA at the category and class level.

**Topic 5: API Drug PA Data and Formulary Information**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; API-USAGE-METRICS
- **Position:** Support in part; Oppose in part
- **Rationale:** Adding drug PA data to APIs can improve transparency, but removing formulary data from Provider Access and Payer-to-Payer APIs would make it harder for clinicians to identify affordable medication options.
- **Specific request:** Add drug PA data to Patient Access, Provider Access, and Payer-to-Payer APIs; monitor burden and update physician payment policy if needed; do not remove drug formulary information from Provider Access and Payer-to-Payer APIs.

**Topic 6: Electronic Event Notifications**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Clarify/Modify
- **Rationale:** Hospices and palliative care teams need timely hospital event notifications but often lack CEHRT and resources.
- **Specific request:** Clarify hospices are included as post-acute providers; encourage notifications to palliative care teams; work with Congress to fund hospice health IT investments and avoid unfunded mandates.

**Topic 7: Step Therapy and DMEPOS RFIs**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Support/Modify
- **Rationale:** Step therapy and DMEPOS PA can harm seriously ill patients and create avoidable clinician burden.
- **Specific request:** Use payer-to-payer medication history to avoid repeated step therapy; digitize tried-and-failed OTC medication data where relevant; use technology and algorithms to reduce DMEPOS PA burden.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S12:** Supports technical standards for medical benefit drug PA using FHIR-based APIs and recommends finalization.
- **S14:** Supports pharmacy benefit drug electronic PA via NCPDP SCRIPT and related NCPDP standards.
- **S16:** Supports specific denial reasons for drug PA denials and explains their value for reconsideration decisions.
- **S20:** Recommends a 24-hour decision timeframe for both standard and expedited drug-related PA requests across impacted payers.
- **S21:** Supports implementation but highlights practice burden and the need for monitoring and enforcement.
- **S28:** Requests future MA alignment so drug PA decisions are due within 24 hours.
- **S29/S34/S35:** Supports updated metrics but recommends greater granularity by service category and drug category/class.
- **S66-S82:** Responds to RFIs on event notifications, step therapy, and DMEPOS by recommending hospice/palliative inclusion, continuity protections, and technology-enabled burden reduction.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Finalize electronic PA requirements for drugs using FHIR APIs or NCPDP SCRIPT depending on benefit type.
2. Finalize specific denial reason requirements for drug PA denials regardless of submission method.
3. Adopt shorter, uniform decision timeframes: 48/24 hours for non-drug requests and 24 hours for drug requests.
4. Expand PA metric reporting to service categories and drug category/class levels.
5. Add drug PA information to Patient Access, Provider Access, and Payer-to-Payer APIs.
6. Retain formulary information in Provider Access and Payer-to-Payer APIs.
7. Clarify hospice and palliative care team inclusion in electronic event notifications and fund needed health IT capacity.
8. Use interoperability to prevent repeated step therapy and reduce DMEPOS PA burden.
9. Establish strong enforcement mechanisms to ensure payer compliance.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** PA delays for serious-illness medications; inconsistent decision timeframes; inadequate granularity in PA reporting; removal of formulary API data; unfunded hospice IT burden.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Delayed symptom relief, patient harm, increased clinician burden, confusion across payer types, and continued workflow fragmentation.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Lack of hospice/palliative CEHRT, vendor gaps, technology upgrade costs, payer compliance, and physician practice capacity.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** A single PA request can take an hour or more of physician or clinical staff time.
- **Studies or research referenced:** No external study is central to the argument; the comment relies on clinical experience and member reports.
- **Examples provided:** Serious illness medications such as long-acting opioids, anti-emetics, bowel medications; DMEPOS needs including walkers, wheelchairs, and hospital beds.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Hospice and palliative care clinicians, seriously ill patients and families, payers, hospitals, hospices, pharmacies, and EHR vendors.
- **Economic implications:** Potential increased costs for practices and hospices from API implementation and event notification infrastructure; potential reduced administrative burden if PA is streamlined.
- **Technical feasibility:** Supportive of standards but concerned about uneven CEHRT availability and implementation burden.
- **Patient care impact:** Strongly positive if finalized with modifications; shorter timeframes and better transparency would reduce delays in pain, symptom, medication, and equipment access.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Supportive with modifications.
- **Tone:** Professional, clinical, collaborative.
- **Priority level:** High.

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "A single prior authorization request can take an hour or more of physician or clinical staff time to process" - Context: Explaining burden on hospice and palliative practices.
2. "Finalizing this proposal would give providers clearer information when assessing whether to seek a reconsideration" - Context: Supporting specific denial reasons.
3. "Each day of treatment delay can result in increased harm" - Context: Justifying shorter PA decision timeframes for seriously ill patients.
4. "No one enters a profession in health care aiming to devote their time to duplicative paperwork" - Context: Describing workforce impact of PA.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - Requests shorter decision timeframes and future MA alignment.
- [x] **COST-RESOURCES** - Discusses IT costs, CEHRT gaps, and physician practice burden.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - Central concern across drug PA, DMEPOS, step therapy, and event notifications.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - Notes CEHRT limitations and API implementation implications.
- [x] **STANDARDS-MATURITY** - Supports FHIR and NCPDP standards while requesting monitoring.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - Emphasizes serious harm from medication and DMEPOS delays.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - Requests CMS, Congress, hospices, hospitals, vendors, and payers coordinate.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - Supports denial reasons, PA metrics, and drug PA API data.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - Focuses on practice workflows, formularies, event notifications, and electronic PA integration.
- [x] **VENDOR-ECOSYSTEM** - Discusses lack of hospice/palliative CEHRT and vendor development gaps.
